## Introduction

Associative forward blocking[^1] refers to the attenuation of learning about
a stimulus-outcome relationship when the stimulus is accompanied by
another one that has already been established to reliably predict that
outcome [@beesley2011; @paskewitz2020].

[^1]: Herein, I will refer to forward blocking simply as _blocking_
    to avoid text cluttering.

Behavioural studies combined with eye-tracking have demonstrated that
blocking occurs in human associative learning and that it can be
accounted for by learned *in*attention to the blocked cue
[@kruschke2005; @beesley2011; @lepelley2007; @wills2007; @luque2018].
Two candidate mechanisms have been proposed to explain this phenomenon:
rapid **attentional shifts**, whereby redirecting attention away from
the blocked cue improves learning, and **attentional competition**,
whereby cues vie for a limited attentional resource [@kruschke2005;
@paskewitz2020].

However, no definitive experiment capable of discriminating between
these two proposed mechanisms has yet been conducted. Using simulations,
@paskewitz2020 derived an experimental design that could, in principle,
adjudicate between the two accounts.

The primary aims of this project are to:

1.  *replicate* the prototypical blocking findings of @beesley2011 in a large
    sample, and
2.  *design and implement an extension* of this paradigm that allows for
    direct comparison between the attentional shift and attentional
    competition accounts of blocking, drawing on the theoretical
    analysis by @paskewitz2020.

## Forward Blocking

Blocking was first described in rodents by @kamin1969 and later
demonstrated in human contingency learning by @dickinson1984 and
@shanks1985. The basic phenomenon can be explained by simple associative
learning models such as the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972].
However, subsequent work suggested that blocking is accompanied by
shifts of attention away from blocked cues, and can thus be better
explained by attentional theories of associative learning [e.g.,
@mackintosh1975; @pearce1980].

Although alternative explanations based on propositional reasoning have
been proposed ***(cite propositional theories)***, learned attention
accounts remain influential and continue to be used in both empirical
and computational work [@paskewitz2020; @paskewitz2023; @kelly2025a;
@kelly2025b][^2]. Rather than adjudicating directly between competing
theoretical frameworks, the present study focuses on subjecting learned
attention models to a severe empirical testing [@mayo1991].

[^2]: **Look for more broad use of the theories. It is surely there,
    they are popular.**

Evidence for attentional mechanisms in blocking comes from several lines
of research, including experimental manipulations of cue competition
[@lepelley2007; @beesley2011], eye-tracking studies of overt attention
[@kruschke2005; @wills2007; @lepelley2007], behavioural measures of
attentional bias [@liu2013; @luque2018], and computational simulations
of attentional learning models [@kruschke2005; @paskewitz2020;
@paskewitz2023; see also @sewell2012 for discussion]. Building on recent
simulation work [@paskewitz2020], the present study designs an
experimental procedure aimed at testing key predictions of
learned-attention theories about blocking and its relation to attention.

In the animal learning literature, blocking is widely regarded as a cornerstone
phenomenon, prompting strong claims such as that *"\[n\]o empirical finding in
the study of animal learning has been of greater theoretical importance than the
phenomenon of blocking."* [@williams1999] However, despite its apparent
robustness and the large body of supporting evidence, @maes2016 were unable to
detect the effect across fifteen replications of previously published rodent
paradigms (see @soto2018 and @maes2018 for discussion of the implications of
these findings). Given this elusive nature of the the blocking phenomenon even
in tightly controlled animal studies, it follows that any attempt to extend
blocking paradigms in human contingency learning should be preceded by a
rigorous replication of the original effect.

## Study designs

Although blocking is often treated as a unitary phenomenon, it can be elicited
using several related but methodologically distinct experimental designs. These
paradigms differ in how they set-up cue competition, control for confounds and
what inferences they permit about underlying mechanisms. @tbl-blocking-original
summarises three representative designs used in prior research [@kruschke2005;
@lepelley2007; @beesley2011; @sewell2012; @luque2018; see also @paskewitz2020;
@paskewitz2023].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-blocking-original
#| tbl-cap: Associational blocking experimental designs used by prior research.

blocking0$designs |>
  mutate(
    design = factor(
      case_when(
        design == "kruschke2005" ~ 1,
        design == "luque2018" ~ 2,
        design == "lepelley2007" ~ 3
      ),
      levels = 1:3,
      labels = c(
        "Kruschke et al. (2005)",
        "Luque et al. (2018)",
        "Le Pelley et al. (2007)"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    ),
    across(ends_with("cue"), toupper)
  ) |>
  arrange(design) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "design") |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "---") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 3", columns = starts_with("stage3")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("outcome") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("preference") ~ "Preferred"
  ) |>
  catlasr::apa_style()
```

The **canonical blocking design** [e.g., @kruschke2005; @sewell2012] captures the core logic of the phenomenon. In Stage 1, a (blocking) cue A is established as a reliable predictor of an outcome (o1). In Stage 2, A is presented in compound with a novel (blocked) cue B, paired with the same outcome. Although B is a valid predictor of o1, it is redundant because A already fully predicts the outcome. In a subsequent Test stage, participants are asked to choose between the outcome (o1) associated with the blocked cue B and an alternative outcome (o2) associated with a control cue D, which was not paired with a pretrained predictor. Participants typically prefer the outcome associated with the control cue. This difference constitutes the canonical blocking effect.

Despite its conceptual simplicity, this design is partially confounded by **cue novelty**. Specifically, the blocked cue B is introduced alongside a
well-established pretrained predictor (A), whereas the control cue D is paired with another novel cue (C). This asymmetry makes it difficult to determine whether reduced learning about B reflects blocking per se or differences in how novel cues are processed within a compound.

One approach to addressing this limitation is to introduce the competitor of the control cue during Stage 1 as a non-predictive pretrained stimulus [e.g., @luque2018]. This manipulation equates novelty across conditions, as both blocked and control cues are paired with pretrained stimuli. However, this solution introduces a different potential confound, as the control cue may appear more predictive by virtue of being compared with a known non-predictive cue, thereby inflating the apparent blocking effect (B-minus-D) without necessarily engaging the same underlying
mechanisms.

A further limitation shared by both designs is that blocked and control cues are consistently paired with the same outcomes. While this allows for strong conclusions about specific cue–outcome associations, it provides limited insight into **cue-specific processing**. In particular, blocking effects observed in these paradigms may arise from interference in learning or memory (i.e., the A-o1 contingency can interfere with learning of B-o1 contingency) without implying changes in attention to the blocked cue itself.

This ambiguity is reflected in computational modelling results. For example, @sewell2012 showed that when fitting the EXIT model [@kruschke2001] to data from the canonical blocking paradigm, the best-fitting attention parameters shrank toward zero, effectively reducing EXIT to the Rescorla–Wagner model [@rescorla1972]. In other words, the canonical design can be accommodated without invoking attentional mechanisms, even when such mechanisms are formally available within the model.

To address these issues, @lepelley2007 introduced a **three-stage** design in which both blocked and control cues are subsequently paired with novel outcomes in Stage 3, in the absence of previously trained competitors. This modification has two important consequences.

First, it attenuates the novelty confound. Because all critical cues are paired with new outcomes in Stage 3, and have comparable prior exposure, differences in learning are less readily attributable to novelty.

Second, and more importantly, the design provides stronger leverage for testing attentional accounts. By requiring previously blocked and control cues to support new learning, it becomes possible to assess whether blocking reflects enduring differences in cue processing. Consistent with this interpretation, @paskewitz2020 showed that the EXIT model fails to reproduce blocking effects in the three-stage paradigm unless it includes at least one attentional mechanism (either rapid attentional shifts or attentional competition). When all attentional mechanisms are removed, the model no longer captures the empirical pattern.

Taken together, these findings suggest that the three-stage design places stronger constraints on theoretical accounts of blocking than canonical paradigms. In particular, it creates conditions under which attentional mechanisms are not merely sufficient but necessary to explain the data within a well-specified computational framework. Building on this logic, the present study adopts and extends this design to directly contrast predictions derived from competing attentional mechanisms.

## Eperiment 2 (extension)

@tbl-blocking-extension shows the experimental design of @beesley2011
after changes .

```{r}
#| label: tbl-blocking-extension
#| tbl-cap: Associational blocking experimental designs proposed by @paskewitz2020.

tibble(
  stage_1_cue = c("A", "C", "E", "G", "I", "L", "O", "R"),
  stage_1_out = paste0("o", rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2)),
  stage_2_cue = c("AB", "CD", "EF", "GH", "JK", "MN", "PQ", "ST"),
  stage_2_out = paste0("o", rep(c(rep(1, 2), rep(2, 2)), 2)),
  stage_3_cue = c("BU", "DV", "FW", "HX", rep(NA, 4)),
  stage_3_out = paste0("o", c(rep(3:4, 2), rep(NA, 4))),
  test_cue = c("BX", "DW", "FV", "HU", "BV", "DU", "FX", "HW"),
  test_out = "?",
  test_pred_shift = paste0("o", rep(3:4, 4)),
  test_pred_comp = paste0("o", rep(4:3, 4))
) |>
  gt() |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "") |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 1", columns = starts_with("stage_1")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 2", columns = starts_with("stage_2")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Stage 3", columns = starts_with("stage_3")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Model Predictions", columns = contains("pred")) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Test", columns = starts_with("test")) |>
  cols_label(
    ends_with("cue") ~ "Cues",
    ends_with("out") ~ "Outcome",
    ends_with("shift") ~ "Shifting (RSWAC)",
    ends_with("comp") ~ "Competition\n(CompAct)"
  ) |>
  catlasr::apa_style()
```
